claim: The TMPRSS2:ERG gene fusion is common in androgen receptor (AR) positive prostate cancers.
source: The TMPRSS2:ERG gene fusion is common in androgen receptor (AR) positive prostate cancers, yet its function remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of prostate cancer research.

claim: ERG recruits PRMT5 to AR-target genes.
source: ERG recruits PRMT5 to AR-target genes, where PRMT5 methylates AR on arginine 761.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A demonstrating ERG-dependent PRMT5 recruitment.

claim: PRMT5 methylates AR on arginine 761.
source: ERG recruits PRMT5 to AR-target genes, where PRMT5 methylates AR on arginine 761.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments showing that only the R761K mutant completely lacked MMA and SDMA modification (Figure 3F).

claim: Methylation of AR at arginine 761 attenuates AR recruitment and transcription of genes expressed in differentiated prostate epithelium.
source: This attenuates AR recruitment and transcription of genes expressed in differentiated prostate epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data showing increased AR recruitment upon PRMT5 knockdown (Figure 2D, 2E) and gene expression data showing upregulation of AR target genes (Figure 2B).

claim: The AR-inhibitory function of PRMT5 is restricted to TMPRSS2:ERG-positive prostate cancer cells.
source: The AR-inhibitory function of PRMT5 is restricted to TMPRSS2:ERG-positive prostate cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by data showing PRMT5 knockdown does not affect AR target gene expression in ERG-negative 22Rv1 or LNCaP cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Mutation of arginine 761 on AR results in a transcriptionally hyperactive AR.
source: Mutation of this methylation site on AR results in a transcriptionally hyperactive AR, suggesting that the proliferative effects of ERG and PRMT5 are mediated through attenuating AR's ability to induce genes normally involved in lineage differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing AR R761K mutant has enhanced recruitment to PSA and increased PSA expression (Figure 4B, C).

claim: AR is an androgen-activated nuclear hormone receptor that regulates normal prostate gland growth and differentiation.
source: AR is an androgen (i.e. testosterone)-activated nuclear hormone receptor that regulates normal prostate gland growth and differentiation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AR function.

claim: In prostate cancer, AR facilitates unregulated proliferation.
source: In PC however, AR facilitates unregulated proliferation (Mills, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mills, 2014.

claim: Many prostate cancers bear chromosomal translocations resulting in aberrant expression of the ETS transcription factor ERG, most commonly through the TMPRSS2:ERG fusion.
source: Many PCs bear chromosomal translocations resulting in aberrant expression of the ETS transcription factor ERG, most commonly through the TMPRSS2:ERG fusion (Shah and Chinnaiyan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shah and Chinnaiyan, 2009.

claim: TMPRSS2:ERG, alone or in combination with additional genetic alterations, promotes prostate tumor formation in mice.
source: TMPRSS2:ERG, alone or in combination with additional genetic alterations, promotes prostate tumor formation in mice (Baena et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013; King et al., 2009; Klezovitch et al., 2008; Mounir et al., 2015; Tomlins et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to mouse model studies.

claim: ERG is recruited to many AR target genes and represses AR-dependent transcription.
source: ERG is recruited to many AR target genes and represses AR-dependent transcription (Yu et al., 2010), suggesting ERG functions at least in part through attenuating AR target gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2010.

claim: AR shRNAs were preferentially depleted from VCaP cells in the shRNA screen.
source: While ERG shRNAs were not in the pool, AR shRNAs were preferentially depleted from VCaP cells, underscoring AR dependence in this cell line.
evidence: This is data from the shRNA screen described in the manuscript.

claim: Thirty-two genes showed VCaP-selective shRNA depletion in the screen.
source: Thirty two (32) genes showing VCaP-selective shRNA depletion (Materials and methods) were considered for further study (Figure 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is data from the shRNA screen shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AR and DNA-PKcs are previously known ERG interactors.
source: Identified proteins (Supplementary file 2) included AR and DNA-PKcs, previously known ERG interactors (Brenner et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brenner et al., 2011 and Yu et al., 2010.

claim: AR and PRMT5 co-immunoprecipitated with ERG but not IgG control in VCaP cells.
source: Of these, AR and PRMT5 were the only proteins that co-immunoprecipitated with ERG but not IgG control; these interactions were not overtly influenced by exposure to an androgen analog (R1881, Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ERG/PRMT5 interaction was observed in 22Rv1 cells ectopically expressing ERG.
source: PRMT5 co-immunoprecipitated with ERG in 22Rv1 cells ectopically expressing ERG.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ERG/PRMT5 interaction was still observed with ERG bearing mutations in the DNA binding domain.
source: This interaction was still observed upon expression of ERG bearing mutations in the DNA binding domain ('Dx', Figure 1C), suggesting DNA binding is not required for the ERG/PRMT5 interaction.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DNA binding is not required for the ERG/PRMT5 interaction.
source: This interaction was still observed upon expression of ERG bearing mutations in the DNA binding domain ('Dx', Figure 1C), suggesting DNA binding is not required for the ERG/PRMT5 interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DNA-binding defective ERG still interacts with PRMT5.

claim: The ERG/PRMT5 interaction can occur in the absence of AR.
source: Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments using overexpressed ERG and PRMT5 in AR-negative 293 and PC3 cells suggest the ERG/PRMT5 interaction can occur in the absence of AR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in AR-negative cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The conserved ETS DNA binding domain of ERG is necessary for co-immunoprecipitation with PRMT5.
source: Further work in 293 cells using truncated ERG constructs suggested that the conserved ETS DNA binding domain of ERG was necessary for the observed co-immunoprecipitation with PRMT5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with ERG deletion mutants shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown caused robust growth inhibition in VCaP cells.
source: Robust growth inhibition was observed in VCaP cells; in contrast PRMT5 knockdown had no growth effects in ERG-negative 22Rv1 cells, and only minor effects in ERG negative LNCaP cells (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown had no growth effects in ERG-negative 22Rv1 cells.
source: Robust growth inhibition was observed in VCaP cells; in contrast PRMT5 knockdown had no growth effects in ERG-negative 22Rv1 cells, and only minor effects in ERG negative LNCaP cells (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown had only minor effects in ERG-negative LNCaP cells.
source: Robust growth inhibition was observed in VCaP cells; in contrast PRMT5 knockdown had no growth effects in ERG-negative 22Rv1 cells, and only minor effects in ERG negative LNCaP cells (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: VCaP, LNCaP, and 22Rv1 cells are all MTAP intact.
source: Deletion of methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP), which is common across cancers, is a major determinant of sensitivity to PRMT5 inhibition (Kryukov et al., 2016; Mavrakis et al., 2016); as VCaP, LNCaP, and 22Rv1 cells are all MTAP intact, the observed sensitivity of VCaP to PRMT5 shRNA is not due to MTAP deletion.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The observed sensitivity of VCaP to PRMT5 shRNA is not due to MTAP deletion.
source: Deletion of methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP), which is common across cancers, is a major determinant of sensitivity to PRMT5 inhibition (Kryukov et al., 2016; Mavrakis et al., 2016); as VCaP, LNCaP, and 22Rv1 cells are all MTAP intact, the observed sensitivity of VCaP to PRMT5 shRNA is not due to MTAP deletion.
evidence: This is inferred from the MTAP status of the cell lines.

claim: PRMT5 is a protein arginine methyltransferase that regulates multiple signaling pathways through mono- and symmetric di-methylation of arginines on its target proteins.
source: PRMT5 is a protein arginine methyltransferase that regulates multiple signaling pathways through the mono- and symmetric di-methylation of arginines on its target proteins (Yang and Bedford, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Yang and Bedford, 2013.

claim: Wild-type PRMT5, but not the G365A/R368A mutant, rescued the effects of PRMT5 knockdown on VCaP cell proliferation.
source: WT PRMT5, but not the G365A/R368A mutant, rescued the effects of PRMT5 knockdown on VCaP cell proliferation (Figure 1G), indicating a requirement for PRMT5 catalytic function to support VCaP proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PRMT5 catalytic function is required to support VCaP proliferation.
source: WT PRMT5, but not the G365A/R368A mutant, rescued the effects of PRMT5 knockdown on VCaP cell proliferation (Figure 1G), indicating a requirement for PRMT5 catalytic function to support VCaP proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing only catalytically active PRMT5 rescues the phenotype.

claim: AR activation was the second most significantly affected pathway upon PRMT5 knockdown in VCaP cells.
source: Among these, AR activation was the second most significantly affected pathway, and is a key pathway in common with previous reports of ERG knockdown in VCaP cells (Chen et al., 2013; Mounir et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Knockdown of either PRMT5 or ERG increased the expression of the AR target genes PSA, NKX3-1 and SLC45A3.
source: Using quantitative PCR of reverse transcribed RNA (qRT-PCR), we confirmed that knockdown of either PRMT5 or ERG increased the expression of the AR target genes PSA, NKX3-1 and SLC45A3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of shRNA-resistant WT PRMT5, but not the G365A/R368A mutant, rescued the effects of PRMT5 knockdown on AR target gene expression.
source: Expression of shRNA-resistant WT PRMT5, but not the G365A/R368A mutant, rescued the effects of PRMT5 knockdown on AR target gene expression (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), demonstrating that PRMT5 methyltransferase activity is required for repression of AR target genes.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PRMT5 methyltransferase activity is required for repression of AR target genes.
source: Expression of shRNA-resistant WT PRMT5, but not the G365A/R368A mutant, rescued the effects of PRMT5 knockdown on AR target gene expression (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), demonstrating that PRMT5 methyltransferase activity is required for repression of AR target genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment showing only catalytically active PRMT5 rescues the phenotype.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown did not affect AR-independent ERG target genes in VCaP.
source: The effect of PRMT5 knockdown was restricted to genes co-regulated by both AR and ERG, as PRMT5 knockdown did not affect previously published (Mounir et al., 2015) AR-independent ERG target genes in VCaP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown did not induce AR target gene expression in ERG negative 22Rv1 or LNCaP PC cells.
source: In addition, PRMT5 knockdown did not induce AR target gene expression in ERG negative 22Rv1 or LNCaP PC cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In 22Rv1 cells, exogenous ERG expression is sufficient to attenuate PSA, NKX3-1, and SLC45A3 expression.
source: In 22Rv1 cells, exogenous ERG expression is sufficient to attenuate PSA, NKX3-1, and SLC45A3 expression (Mounir et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mounir et al., 2015.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown restored the expression of PSA, NKX3-1, and SLC45A3 to baseline levels in 22Rv1 cells expressing ERG.
source: Under these conditions, PRMT5 knockdown restored the expression of these genes to baseline levels, yet had no effect on their expression in the background of the DNA-binding defective (i.e. inactive) ERG mutant ('Dx', Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: PRMT5's ability to repress AR function is dependent on ERG.
source: These data indicate that PRMT5's ability to repress AR function is dependent on ERG.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PRMT5 knockdown only affects AR target genes in the presence of functional ERG.

claim: ERG knockdown in VCaP reduced its recruitment to binding sites on PSA and NKX3-1.
source: ERG knockdown in VCaP reduced its recruitment to previously characterized (Wei et al., 2010) binding sites on both genes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PRMT5 is recruited to ERG binding sites on PSA and NKX3-1.
source: We also observed PRMT5 recruitment to these same sites, which was dramatically reduced upon ERG knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PRMT5 recruitment to PSA and NKX3-1 was dramatically reduced upon ERG knockdown.
source: We also observed PRMT5 recruitment to these same sites, which was dramatically reduced upon ERG knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ERG expression in 22Rv1 cells induced PRMT5 recruitment to PSA and NKX3-1.
source: Conversely, ERG expression in 22Rv1 cells induced PRMT5 recruitment to these same sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown reduced its own recruitment to PSA and NKX3-1 but had virtually no effect on ERG recruitment.
source: In VCaP, PRMT5 knockdown reduced its own recruitment to both genes but had virtually no effect on ERG recruitment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ERG expression in 22Rv1 reduced AR recruitment to PSA and NKX3-1.
source: As expected (Yu et al., 2010), ERG expression in 22Rv1 reduced AR recruitment to both genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), and ERG knockdown in VCaP increased AR recruitment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data and citation to Yu et al., 2010.

claim: ERG knockdown in VCaP increased AR recruitment to PSA and NKX3-1.
source: As expected (Yu et al., 2010), ERG expression in 22Rv1 reduced AR recruitment to both genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), and ERG knockdown in VCaP increased AR recruitment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown strongly induced AR recruitment to PSA and NKX3-1.
source: Like ERG, PRMT5 knockdown in VCaP strongly induced AR recruitment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown increased the recruitment of AR at a subset of peaks (6% of the total Cistrome).
source: In agreement with directed ChIP experiments, AR ChIP-seq demonstrated that PRMT5 knockdown increased the recruitment of AR at a subset of peaks (6% p-val 0.01, q-val 0.151), (Figure 2E), but did not significantly affect ERG binding on the same set of sites.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PRMT5 knockdown did not significantly affect ERG binding at sites where AR binding increased.
source: In agreement with directed ChIP experiments, AR ChIP-seq demonstrated that PRMT5 knockdown increased the recruitment of AR at a subset of peaks (6% p-val 0.01, q-val 0.151), (Figure 2E), but did not significantly affect ERG binding on the same set of sites.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: ERG expression in 22Rv1 cells did not alter H4R3me2s levels at the PSA or NKX3-1 loci.
source: However, ERG expression in 22Rv1 cells did not alter H4R3me2s levels at the PSA or NKX3-1 loci (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MMA and SDMA signals were detected in AR immunoprecipitates from VCaP cells.
source: MMA and SDMA signals were indeed detected in AR immunoprecipitates from VCaP cells, and were reduced following knockdown of either ERG or PRMT5 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MMA and SDMA signals on AR were reduced following knockdown of either ERG or PRMT5 in VCaP cells.
source: MMA and SDMA signals were indeed detected in AR immunoprecipitates from VCaP cells, and were reduced following knockdown of either ERG or PRMT5 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunoprecipitated AR from TMPRSS2:ERG mouse prostates showed high mono- and symmetric di-methylation levels compared to wild-type controls.
source: Like VCaP, immunoprecipitated AR from TMPRSS2:ERG mouse prostates showed high mono- (MMA) and symmetric di-methylation (SDMA) levels compared to wild-type controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data from mouse tissues shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LNCaP cells do not show any SDMA signal on AR.
source: On the other hand, LNCaP cells, which bear a translocation in the ETS factor ETV1, do not show any SDMA signal on AR, and show reduced levels of MMA versus VCaP (Figure 3C), suggesting that AR symmetric dimethylation is unique to ERG versus ETV1.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: AR symmetric dimethylation is unique to ERG versus ETV1.
source: On the other hand, LNCaP cells, which bear a translocation in the ETS factor ETV1, do not show any SDMA signal on AR, and show reduced levels of MMA versus VCaP (Figure 3C), suggesting that AR symmetric dimethylation is unique to ERG versus ETV1.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of AR methylation in ERG-positive versus ETV1-positive cells.

claim: ERG expression increased MMA and SDMA signals on wild-type AR but not the truncated variant in 22Rv1 cells.
source: In these cells, ERG expression increased MMA and SDMA signals on wild-type AR but not the truncated variant, and these ERG-dependent signals were reduced upon PRMT5 knockdown (Figure 3D), suggesting the AR LBD is mono- and symmetrically di-methylated in an ERG- and PRMT5-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The AR LBD is mono- and symmetrically di-methylated in an ERG- and PRMT5-dependent manner.
source: In these cells, ERG expression increased MMA and SDMA signals on wild-type AR but not the truncated variant, and these ERG-dependent signals were reduced upon PRMT5 knockdown (Figure 3D), suggesting the AR LBD is mono- and symmetrically di-methylated in an ERG- and PRMT5-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only full-length AR (containing LBD) shows ERG-dependent methylation.

claim: PRMT5 activity was observed in the presence of AR LBD as substrate.
source: PRMT5 activity, as judged by production of SAH (the by-product of SAM-dependent substrate methylation), was observed in the presence of AR LBD as substrate, but not in the presence of ERG ETS DNA binding domain or pointed (PNT) domain.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro methyltransferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PRMT5 activity was not observed in the presence of ERG ETS DNA binding domain or pointed (PNT) domain as substrate.
source: PRMT5 activity, as judged by production of SAH (the by-product of SAM-dependent substrate methylation), was observed in the presence of AR LBD as substrate, but not in the presence of ERG ETS DNA binding domain or pointed (PNT) domain.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro methyltransferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PRMT5 activity in the presence of AR LBD further increased with the addition of ERG ETS domain protein to the reaction.
source: PRMT5 activity in the presence of AR LBD further increased with the addition of ERG ETS domain protein to the reaction, but not with PNT domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro methyltransferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PRMT1 showed no activity in the presence of AR LBD.
source: Unlike PRMT5, purified PRMT1 showed no activity in the presence of AR LBD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro methyltransferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: PRMT5 activity on AR was reduced with the addition of the tool PRMT inhibitor AMI-1.
source: PRMT5 activity on AR, in the absence or presence of ERG ETS domain, was reduced with the addition of the tool PRMT inhibitor AMI-1 (Cheng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro methyltransferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: AR LBD is a substrate of the PRMT5 enzyme in vitro.
source: Together this data indicates that AR LBD is a substrate of the PRMT5 enzyme in vitro, and that the ERG ETS domain can facilitate greater PRMT5 activity on AR.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro methyltransferase assay results.

claim: The ERG ETS domain can facilitate greater PRMT5 activity on AR.
source: Together this data indicates that AR LBD is a substrate of the PRMT5 enzyme in vitro, and that the ERG ETS domain can facilitate greater PRMT5 activity on AR.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro methyltransferase assay results showing increased activity with ERG ETS domain.

claim: Only the AR R761K mutant completely lacked MMA and SDMA of AR in the presence of ERG.
source: All mutants were expressed at equivalent levels to wild-type AR (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C). Only one AR mutant, R761K, completely lacked MMA and SDMA of AR in the presence of ERG (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Arginine 761 is the likely target of ERG- and PRMT5-dependent AR methylation.
source: This demonstrates that arginine 761 is the likely target of ERG- and PRMT5-dependent AR methylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing only R761K mutation eliminates methylation.

claim: Strong proximity ligation signals for AR/SDMA were detected in RWPE-1 nuclei upon expression of wild-type AR and exposure to R1881.
source: We detected strong proximity signals in RWPE-1 nuclei upon expression of wild-type AR and exposure to R1881 (which stimulates nuclear translocation of AR) that were dependent upon ERG expression.
evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: AR/SDMA proximity signals were not detected in the AR R761K mutant cell line.
source: These signals were not detected in the AR R761K mutant cell line (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: R761 methylation on AR may affect LBD interactions with the DNA binding domain.
source: Available structural information (Chandra V et al., 2008; Emsley et al., 2010; Helsen et al., 2012) (see Materials and methods) suggests R761 methylation on AR may affect LBD interactions with the DNA binding domain (DBD, Figure 4A), resulting in altered DNA binding and gene activation.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and inference from published structural data.

claim: The AR R761K mutant showed enhanced recruitment to PSA relative to WT AR.
source: Relative to WT AR, the AR R761K mutant showed enhanced recruitment to PSA and increased PSA expression.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The AR R761K mutant showed increased PSA expression relative to WT AR.
source: Relative to WT AR, the AR R761K mutant showed enhanced recruitment to PSA and increased PSA expression.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: R761K mutation prevented ERG-dependent attenuation of AR recruitment to PSA.
source: Moreover, R761K mutation prevented ERG-dependent attenuation of AR recruitment to PSA and PSA expression (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: R761K mutation prevented ERG-dependent attenuation of PSA expression.
source: Moreover, R761K mutation prevented ERG-dependent attenuation of AR recruitment to PSA and PSA expression (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The AR R761K mutation did not affect overall AR protein levels.
source: In contrast to these effects, the AR R761K mutation did not affect overall AR protein levels, the ability of AR to shuttle into the nucleus upon R1881 induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), or the levels of ERG or PRMT5 recruitment to PSA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The AR R761K mutation did not affect the ability of AR to shuttle into the nucleus upon R1881 induction.
source: In contrast to these effects, the AR R761K mutation did not affect overall AR protein levels, the ability of AR to shuttle into the nucleus upon R1881 induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), or the levels of ERG or PRMT5 recruitment to PSA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The AR R761K mutation did not affect the levels of ERG or PRMT5 recruitment to PSA.
source: In contrast to these effects, the AR R761K mutation did not affect overall AR protein levels, the ability of AR to shuttle into the nucleus upon R1881 induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), or the levels of ERG or PRMT5 recruitment to PSA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: R761 methylation attenuates ligand-dependent AR activation.
source: These results indicate R761 methylation mediated through ERG and PRMT5 attenuates ligand-dependent AR activation, likely through modulating interactions between the LBD and DBD.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing R761K mutation increases AR activity.

claim: RWPE-1 cells expressing AR R761K were more prone to R1881-induced growth arrest than cells expressing wild-type AR.
source: However, we noted that RWPE-1 cells expressing AR R761K, despite increased AR activity, were more prone to R1881-induced growth arrest (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: VCaP cells expressing AR R761K showed increased PSA expression relative to WT AR.
source: Despite transcriptional hyperactivity, as judged by increased PSA expression relative to either WT or an irrelevant R789K mutant AR, VCaP cells expressing AR R761K proliferated poorly in reduced-androgen media (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: VCaP cells expressing AR R761K proliferated poorly in reduced-androgen media.
source: Despite transcriptional hyperactivity, as judged by increased PSA expression relative to either WT or an irrelevant R789K mutant AR, VCaP cells expressing AR R761K proliferated poorly in reduced-androgen media (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A primary effect of ERG in facilitating PC proliferation is modulating AR function.
source: Our results indicate that a primary effect of ERG in facilitating PC proliferation is modulating AR function.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data showing ERG recruits PRMT5 to methylate AR and modulate its activity.

claim: ERG- and PRMT5-dependent methylation of R761 on AR reduces AR recruitment to genes that would otherwise induce differentiation.
source: We propose that ERG- and PRMT5-dependent methylation of R761 on AR reduces AR recruitment to genes that would otherwise induce differentiation, yet R761 methylation allows sufficient AR function to promote proliferation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective experimental data.

claim: R761 methylation allows sufficient AR function to promote proliferation.
source: We propose that ERG- and PRMT5-dependent methylation of R761 on AR reduces AR recruitment to genes that would otherwise induce differentiation, yet R761 methylation allows sufficient AR function to promote proliferation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective experimental data.
